---
title: "Accuracy and speed"
---

`stateMINT` stands in for `malariasimulation`, so the question that decides whether it can be
used is how closely it reproduces the simulator on parameter sets it was never trained on. We
compare the two on the held-out split, first as trajectories and then as a distribution of
error, and we finish by measuring what a prediction costs.

{{< include ../_truth-setup.qmd >}}

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

plt.style.use("styles/mint.mplstyle")

traj = pd.read_csv("data/validation/trajectories.csv")
summary = pd.read_csv("data/validation/summary.csv").iloc[0]
run_mae = pd.read_csv("data/validation/run_mae.csv")
latency = pd.read_csv("data/validation/latency.csv")
```

## The held-out split

The emulator was trained on a library of `malariasimulation` runs, split by parameter set into
70% training, 15% validation and 15% test. The figures below use the test split only, taken
from the split file that shipped with the trained weights, so every trajectory belongs to a
parameter set the model never saw in any epoch.

```{python}
#| echo: false
print(f"held-out runs      {int(summary['n_runs']):,}")
print(f"time points        {int(summary['n_points']):,}")
```

## Trajectories

Five held-out runs spanning the 10th to the 90th percentile of EIR are plotted below, with the
simulator drawn as a dashed white line over the emulator's solid blue one.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Out-of-sample prevalence under five held-out parameter sets. The dashed white line is malariasimulation and the solid blue line is stateMINT."
#| fig-alt: "Five panels of prevalence over time. In each, the emulator's solid coloured line lies almost exactly under the simulator's dashed white ground-truth line, before and after the campaign."
panels = sorted(traj["panel"].unique())
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(panels), figsize=(14.5, 3.1), sharey=True)

for ax, p in zip(axes, panels):
    d = traj[traj["panel"] == p]
    ax.plot(d["years_from_campaign"], d["emulator"], color="#3987e5", lw=2.6,
            label="stateMINT", zorder=2)
    ax.plot(d["years_from_campaign"], d["truth"], color="#ffffff", lw=1.5,
            ls=(0, (4, 2.6)), label="malariasimulation", zorder=3)
    ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=0.9, alpha=0.6, zorder=1)
    ax.set_title(f"EIR {d['eir'].iloc[0]:g}", fontsize=9.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("years from campaign")

axes[0].set_ylabel("prevalence")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="best")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Because the truth is dashed over the top of the emulator, any disagreement between the two
would appear as the white line separating from the blue. The two stay close across all five
panels, and the emulator tracks the pre-campaign equilibrium, the drop when the intervention
lands, and the shape of the recovery, including the sharp annual oscillation of the strongly
seasonal setting in the right-hand panel.

Note that the simulator traces are noisy. An individual-based model produces a stochastic
trajectory and the emulator predicts the smooth expectation through it, so part of the residual
here is the simulator's own Monte Carlo noise rather than emulator error.

## Pipeline error and emulator error

The figure above gives the emulator the EIR the simulator itself was run at. A user does not
have that number and has to estimate it from a prevalence survey, so the error they see is the
error of the whole chain rather than of the emulator alone. To separate the two we plot three
held-out parameter sets with both paths drawn.

The white line is `malariasimulation`, averaged over the stochastic runs drawn in grey behind
it. The red line is the full pipeline, which starts from the measured year-9 prevalence and
inverts it to an EIR with `estimint` before running `stateMINT` forward. The green dashed line
is `stateMINT` given the simulator's own EIR. The gap between green and white is therefore the
cost of the emulation, while the gap between red and green is the cost of the inversion.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Three held-out parameter sets. White is malariasimulation averaged over the grey stochastic runs, red is the full pipeline from a measured prevalence, and green dashed is the emulator given the simulator's own EIR."
#| fig-alt: "Two rows of three panels, prevalence above and clinical cases below. In each panel the red pipeline line and the green dashed emulator line both track the white simulator average closely, within the spread of the grey individual runs."
cases = [16, 20, 27]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(13.5, 6.0), sharex=True)

for col, cid in enumerate(cases):
    truth_panel(axes[0, col], cid, "prevalence")
    truth_panel(axes[1, col], cid, "cases")
    axes[0, col].set_title(truth_title(cid), fontsize=9)
    axes[1, col].set_xlabel("years from campaign")

axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("prevalence")
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("cases per 1000 per day")
axes[0, 0].plot([], [], color=TRUTH, lw=3.4, label="malariasimulation")
axes[0, 0].plot([], [], color=PIPELINE, lw=1.8, label="pipeline")
axes[0, 0].plot([], [], color=EMULATOR, lw=1.5, ls=(0, (4, 2.6)), label="emulator at true EIR")
axes[0, 0].legend(fontsize=7.5, loc="best")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Each panel fails in a different way, and the two failures are worth telling apart. In the left
panel all three lines coincide, which is the case where the inversion recovers the EIR and the
emulator reproduces the simulator. In the middle panel the red line runs above the white one
while the green line stays on it, because `estimint` estimated an EIR of 12.5 against a true
11.8 and the emulator was then run forward from a transmission intensity that was too high. In
the right panel red and green coincide with each other but both sit slightly below the
simulator once the campaign lands, so there the residual belongs to the emulator rather than to
the inversion.

```{python}
#| echo: false
m = truth_meta[truth_meta.predictor == "prevalence"].copy()
m["setting"] = m.description.str.replace(" - ", ", ", regex=False)
m = m[["setting", "true_eir", "est_eir", "mae_emulator", "mae_pipeline"]]
m.columns = ["setting", "true EIR", "estimated EIR", "MAE, emulator", "MAE, pipeline"]
m.style.hide(axis="index").format({"true EIR": "{:.2f}", "estimated EIR": "{:.2f}",
                                   "MAE, emulator": "{:.4f}", "MAE, pipeline": "{:.4f}"})
```

The middle setting carries a pipeline error roughly three times its emulator error, and the
other two carry pipeline and emulator errors that are the same size. This is the general shape
of the stack. Where the inversion is accurate the emulator sets the floor on the error, and
where the inversion is not, it dominates, which is why the prevalence survey a run starts from
matters more to the answer than the emulator does.

## Error on the held-out set

```{python}
#| echo: false
metrics = pd.DataFrame([
    ("Mean absolute error",        f"{summary['mae_mean']:.4f}"),
    ("Median absolute error",      f"{summary['mae_median']:.4f}"),
    ("90th percentile of MAE",     f"{summary['mae_p90']:.4f}"),
    ("Worst run",                  f"{summary['mae_max']:.4f}"),
    ("RMSE",                       f"{summary['rmse_mean']:.4f}"),
    ("Mean bias",                  f"{summary['bias_mean']:+.5f}"),
    ("R²",                         f"{summary['r2']:.5f}"),
], columns=["", "prevalence"])
metrics.style.hide(axis="index")
```

These numbers are in prevalence units, so a mean absolute error of 0.0044 means the emulator's
prevalence is typically within about 0.4 percentage points of the simulator's, and a run at 30%
prevalence is reproduced somewhere between roughly 29.6% and 30.4%. The mean bias of about
−0.0004 says the emulator is not systematically high or low.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of per-run mean absolute error across the held-out split."
#| fig-alt: "A histogram of per-run mean absolute error, concentrated near zero with a short right tail."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.2))
ax.hist(run_mae["mae"], bins=60, color="#199e70", edgecolor="none")
ax.axvline(summary["mae_median"], color="#e66767", lw=1.6,
           label=f"median {summary['mae_median']:.4f}")
ax.axvline(summary["mae_p90"], color="#c98500", lw=1.6, ls="--",
           label=f"90th pct {summary['mae_p90']:.4f}")
ax.set_xlabel("mean absolute error, per held-out run")
ax.set_ylabel("runs")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

The distribution is tight and right-skewed, and the worst single run in the held-out set is off
by about 0.057, which is under six percentage points of prevalence.

That error sets the resolution of any comparison between campaigns. Differences smaller than
about half a percentage point of prevalence sit inside the emulator's own error and should not
be read as real.

## Speed

A `malariasimulation` run over the same 12 simulated years takes minutes, while the emulator is
a single forward pass.

```{python}
#| echo: false
lat = latency.copy()
lat.columns = ["batch size", "total (ms)", "per scenario (ms)"]
lat.round(2).style.hide(axis="index")
```

On CPU a single isolated call costs more per scenario than a batched one, and most of that
difference is fixed dispatch overhead rather than computation. Amortised across a batch the cost
settles at a few milliseconds per scenario, so passing a list to `predict` or `run_scenarios` is
markedly cheaper than looping over it, which is why the API takes a list.

On a GPU the same forward pass is roughly six times faster again (measured on an NVIDIA L40S).
For a scenario grid the CPU is entirely adequate, and the GPU matters when you are sweeping
thousands of parameter sets.

A campaign comparison that would once have been a batch job on a cluster now runs inside a loop,
or behind a web form, at interactive speed.
